bw: Period of contraction while the heart pumps blood into circulation
tp: Systole is contraction and diastole is relaxation while the chambers fill. Both atria and ventricles go through both.

ww.Diastole: Diastole is the period of relaxation as the chambers fill.
ww.Isovolumic relaxation: Isovolumic relaxation is just the early phase of ventricular diastole.

evidence: The period of contraction that the heart undergoes while it pumps blood into circulation is called systole.

bw: Atria and ventricles both relaxed
Tricuspid and mitral valves open
Share of ventricular filling that occurs passively
tp: Atrial contraction supplies the remaining 20–30 percent of ventricular filling.

ww.About 20–30 percent: That is the contribution of atrial systole (the atrial kick).
ww.About 50 percent: The source gives about 70–80 percent for passive filling, not half.

evidence: Approximately 70–80 percent of ventricular filling occurs by this method.

bw: Atrial contraction, the “atrial kick”
Adds the remaining ventricular filling
tp: At the start of atrial systole the ventricles are already about 70–80 percent full from passive inflow.

ww.70–80 percent of ventricular filling: That is the share from passive filling before atrial systole.
ww.5–10 percent of ventricular filling: The source puts the atrial kick at 20–30 percent.

evidence: Atrial contraction, also referred to as the “atrial kick,” contributes the remaining 20–30 percent of filling (see Figure 19.27).

bw: Volume of blood in the ventricles just before ventricular contraction
About 130 mL in a resting standing adult
Also called preload
tp: EDV is measured at the end of atrial systole, just before ventricular contraction.

ww.End systolic volume (ESV): ESV is the 50–60 mL left in the ventricle after contraction.
ww.Stroke volume: Stroke volume is the 70–80 mL ejected with each beat.

evidence: This volume is known as the end diastolic volume (EDV) or preload.

bw: First phase of ventricular systole
Ventricular pressure rising
Atrioventricular valves closed and semilunar valves not yet open
Ventricular volume unchanged
tp: Blood is not ejected in this phase, so chamber volume stays constant while pressure climbs above atrial pressure.

ww.Ventricular ejection phase: Ejection is the second phase, when the semilunar valves open and blood leaves.
ww.Late ventricular diastole: Late ventricular diastole is relaxation and filling, not contraction.

evidence: Consequently, this initial phase of ventricular systole is known as isovolumic contraction, also called isovolumetric contraction (see Figure 19.27).

bw: Amount of blood each ventricle pumps per contraction
Normally 70–80 mL
tp: With an EDV of about 130 mL and a stroke volume of 70–80 mL, 50–60 mL remains in the ventricle as the ESV.

ww.End systolic volume (ESV): ESV is the blood left in the ventricle after contraction.
ww.End diastolic volume (EDV): EDV is the volume in the ventricle before contraction, about 130 mL.

evidence: Stroke volume will normally be in the range of 70–80 mL.

bw: Blood remaining in the ventricle after contraction
About 50–60 mL
tp: ESV equals EDV minus stroke volume.

ww.Stroke volume: Stroke volume is the blood ejected, not the blood left behind.
ww.End diastolic volume (EDV): EDV is the volume before contraction.

evidence: This volume of blood is known as the end systolic volume (ESV).

bw: Small dip seen in blood pressure tracings
Blood flows back toward the heart as ventricular pressure falls
Semilunar valves close
tp: The dicrotic notch appears in early ventricular diastole, when ventricular pressure drops below that in the pulmonary trunk and aorta.

ww.QRS complex: The QRS complex is an ECG wave of ventricular depolarization, not a feature of pressure tracings.
ww.S3 heart sound: S3 is a rarely heard third heart sound, not a dip in a pressure tracing.

evidence: When pressure within the ventricles drops below pressure in both the pulmonary trunk and aorta, blood flows back toward the heart, producing the dicrotic notch (small dip) seen in blood pressure tracings.

bw: First heart sound, a “lub”
Closing of the atrioventricular valves during ventricular contraction
tp: In a healthy heart only S1 and S2 are normally audible.

ww.S2: S2 is the “dub” of the semilunar valves closing.
ww.S3: S3 is rarely heard in healthy people.

evidence: S1 is the sound created by the closing of the atrioventricular valves during ventricular contraction and is normally described as a “lub,” or first heart sound.

bw: Second heart sound, a “dub”
Closing of the semilunar valves during ventricular diastole
tp: S1 is the closure of the AV valves; S2 is the closure of the pulmonary and aortic valves.

ww.S1: S1 is the AV valves closing during ventricular contraction.
ww.S4: S4 comes from atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle and occurs before S1.

evidence: The second heart sound, S2, is the sound of the closing of the semilunar valves during ventricular diastole and is described as a “dub” (Figure 19.29).

bw: Third heart sound
Rarely heard in healthy individuals
Heard later in life may indicate congestive heart failure
tp: S3 may be heard in youth, some athletes and pregnant women. If heard later in life it warrants further tests.

ww.S1: S1 is always heard in a normal heart.
ww.S4: S4 results from atrial contraction into a stiff or hypertrophic ventricle.

evidence: There is a third heart sound, S3, but it is rarely heard in healthy individuals.

bw: Atrial contraction pushing blood into a stiff or hypertrophic ventricle
Occurs before S1
Indicates failure of the left ventricle
tp: S4, S1 and S2 together are the “Tennessee gallop”; S1, S2 and S3 are the “Kentucky gallop”.

ww.S2: S2 is the semilunar valves closing and occurs after S1.
ww.S3: S3 may be blood flowing into the atria, sloshing in the ventricle, or tensing of the chordae tendineae.

evidence: The fourth heart sound, S4, results from the contraction of the atria pushing blood into a stiff or hypertrophic ventricle, indicating failure of the left ventricle.

bw: Unusual sound from the heart
Caused by turbulent blood flow
Graded on a scale of 1 to 6
tp: Grade 1 is the most common, hardest to detect and least serious; grade 6 is the most severe.

ww.Gallop: A gallop is the cadence of S3 or S4 heard with S1 and S2, not a graded turbulent-flow sound.
ww.Dicrotic notch: The dicrotic notch is a dip on a pressure tracing, not a sound.

evidence: The term murmur is used to describe an unusual sound coming from the heart that is caused by the turbulent flow of blood.

bw: Patient asked to breathe deeply during auscultation
Inhalation increases blood flow into the right side of the heart
tp: Expiration partially restricts blood flow into the left side of the heart and may amplify left-sided murmurs.

ww.May amplify left-sided heart murmurs: That is the effect of expiration, not inhalation.
ww.Abolishes all heart murmurs: Deep breathing tends to amplify murmurs, which helps hear them.

evidence: Inhalation increases blood flow into the right side of the heart and may increase the amplitude of right-sided heart murmurs.

bw: Expiration during auscultation
Partially restricts blood flow into the left side of the heart
tp: Inhalation increases flow into the right heart and may amplify right-sided murmurs.

ww.May amplify right-sided heart murmurs: That is the effect of inhalation, not expiration.
ww.Abolishes all heart murmurs: Breathing changes tend to amplify murmurs rather than abolish them.

evidence: Expiration partially restricts blood flow into the left side of the heart and may amplify left-sided heart murmurs.

bw: Left ventricle generates much more pressure than the right
Both ventricles pump the same stroke volume
ans: The pressure in the aorta is much higher than in the pulmonary trunk
d: The left ventricle has a smaller stroke volume
The mitral valve is wider than the tricuspid valve
tp: Despite the pressure difference, both ventricles pump the same amount of blood per beat.

ww.The left ventricle has a smaller stroke: The source says both ventricles pump the same amount of blood.
ww.The mitral valve is wider than the tricu: The source explains the pressure difference by aortic pressure, not valve size.

evidence: Pressure generated by the left ventricle will be appreciably greater than the pressure generated by the right ventricle, since the existing pressure in the aorta will be so much higher.

bw: Blood flows into the left atrium from
d: The superior and inferior venae cavae
tp: The right atrium receives blood from the venae cavae and the coronary sinus.

ww.The superior and inferior venae cavae: The venae cavae drain into the right atrium.
ww.The coronary sinus: The coronary sinus drains into the right atrium.

evidence: Blood flows into the left atrium from the four pulmonary veins.
